During my senior year of college all of my friends started calling me Michaelsoft. Even the pretty girls we'd hang out with would call me Michaelsoft. Trust me, they didn't call me that because it sounded cool. They all knew I just came back from my internship in Redmond and would be headed back full time after graduation. Thank god people forgot that nickname. 

This summer I crossed the 10 year mark at the company. My entire career, in one place. Over the past decade I had to learn a lot of lessons the hard way. Here are a few thoughts as I look back on my career so far. 

### 1. Keep the Main Thing, the Main Thing
### 2. Meetings Are Empty Calories

When in doubt, people set up meetings. They might even set up a recurring meeting, lucky you! Pretty soon your day is now 5 hours of back to back meetings. I try to avoid meetings like the plague. Any meeting that's over three people needs a strong reason for my presence, or else I will skip it. 

Meetings should be called to help make decisions about what to do next. Most of the time they are a way to provide updates. Even worse is when meetings are set as a forcing function to make sure work is getting done. Yuck. 

Thankfully AI can now attend most meetings for you. So nowadays unless I'm speaking for +30% of the time in a meeting I will most likely not attend and have my AI tools comb through the recording for any action items on my part. 

### 3. Ask for What You Want

### 4. Be You

The longer you work somewhere, the more tiring it becomes to show an unauthentic version of yourself. You can wear the mask for a while, maybe even years, but over time that will grind you down. This leaves you no other choice than to be the most authentic version of yourself. 

Can't stand after work happy hour with the boss? Don't go. Prefer to start work at 7am and finish by 3pm? Don't feel bad walking out the door early. Need 4 hour blocks of uninterrupted morning deep work? Skip the weekly staff meeting. Think the new AI initiative is a waste of time and money? Speak up. You do you. As long as your manager knows who you are and that you get stuff done, then the rest is not important. 

You are the best person at the world at being you, so don't hide it. Lean into it. If that hurts your current job then get a new one that suits you better.

### 5. Mission Over Managers

Ok let me do the math over the last 10 years. 

- 4 different jobs: 3 were 6 month rotations in the Finance Rotation Program
- 7 title changes: yes you read that right
- 10 managers: in one record year I had 4 different managers

Re-orgs are the norm in the big corporate machine world.
